items.question: How did you react to OpenAI’s demonstration of making a game with ordinary language and GPT’s ability to write poems, given your understanding of programming?
items.object: OpenAI’s natural-language game demo and GPT’s creative writing capabilities
items.answer: After ChatGPT came out, I remember very clearly seeing a video on YouTube. It was an OpenAI team demo where they used ordinary language to say, make a little game or something. I remember clearly that I chuckled to myself when I saw it: this definitely will not work—how can human language be used as a program? I had done programming competitions before, and in my mind programs were rigid: if you input one, you cannot input two. I found it especially surprising. items.question: What is your reasoning behind the attention projection mixing design in your paper “Attention Projection Mixing with Exogenous Encodes”?
items.object: The design of attention projection mixing in “Attention Projection Mixing with Exogenous Encodes”
items.answer: The broad framework of the paper is Value Potential Learning: it mixes the values from attention in the first layer into several subsequent layers. My paper found that you can use RMSNorm on these mixtures. For example, the value can be extended to the key and query, and the result is better. This is because the first layer’s value has to do two things: first, be used in that layer; second, be added into later layers for mixing. I found that these two functions can be separated: double the width of the first layer’s attention projection, then split it in half. One half is used for that layer, and the other half for later mixing. Then the result is better.
